title: Verification and Iterative Improvement
summary: Check AI output with evidence, diagnose the kind of failure, and improve the workflow without hiding uncertainty.
objectives: Match verification strength to claim type, volatility, and consequence.
Decompose a response into claims and attach the nearest practical evidence.
Diagnose whether a miss comes from the task, context, prompt, model, tool, or review process.
Version and compare prompt changes against representative cases.

sections.title: Verify claims, not confidence
paragraphs: Break a response into checkable units: factual claims, calculations, quotations, classifications, code behavior, recommendations, and actions. Each needs evidence suited to what it asserts.
Use current authoritative sources for volatile facts, recompute calculations, run code and tests, compare quotations with originals, and obtain domain review for consequential judgments.
sections.callout: The nearest evidence is usually stronger than another fluent summary.

sections.title: Scale verification to consequence and uncertainty
paragraphs: Low-consequence brainstorming may need only a usefulness review. Moderate-consequence work benefits from source comparison, examples, tests, and edge cases. High-consequence decisions require current authoritative evidence, independent review, domain expertise, and a safe approval boundary.
Verification should be planned before generation so time, tools, and responsible reviewers are available.

code.label: Verification-plan template
code.code:
Output use: [DECISION OR ACTION]
Claims to check: [FACTS, MATH, QUOTES, CODE, JUDGMENT]
Consequence if wrong: [LOW, MODERATE, HIGH]
Evidence per claim: [SOURCE, TEST, CALCULATION, REVIEW]
Independent check: [WHO OR WHAT]
Pass criteria: [OBSERVABLE RESULT]
Failure action: [CORRECT, ESCALATE, OR STOP]

sections.title: Diagnose before changing the prompt
paragraphs: A failed result may come from an unclear objective, missing or bad context, contradictory instructions, unsuitable examples, a weak output contract, provider capability, tool failure, or an inadequate review method. Adding more words to the prompt will not fix every cause.
Record the failure category and the smallest change that addresses it. Keep safety and approval boundaries stable while testing changes.

sections.title: Improve with representative cases
paragraphs: Save a small evaluation set containing normal, boundary, missing-data, conflicting-source, privacy-sensitive, and adversarial-like cases. Compare the previous and revised workflow on the same cases.
Version the prompt, context recipe, output contract, model or product, and evaluation result. A change is an improvement only when it raises the intended quality without unacceptable regressions.
sections.callout: Do not optimize one impressive example and call the workflow reliable.

activity.title: Verify a response and improve the workflow
instructions: Choose an AI response containing at least three different claim types.
List each claim, its consequence if wrong, and the nearest practical evidence needed to check it.
Record every failed check and classify its likely cause as task, context, prompt, model, tool, or review.
Change one controllable element, rerun the original case plus two boundary cases, and compare results.
evidence: A claim-to-evidence table with consequence, verification result, and failure action.
A before-and-after comparison that records one change, three cases, improvements, regressions, and remaining uncertainty.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which failure initially looked like a prompt problem but came from another part of the workflow?

cues.text: Decompose one polished paragraph into facts, calculation, quotation, recommendation, and action, then pair each with different evidence.
Connect claim types to source comparison, recomputation, original quotation, test execution, or expert review.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A text mapping pairs facts with authoritative sources, math with recomputation, quotations with originals, code with tests, and consequential judgment with domain review. Reduced-motion mode shows all mappings.

cues.text: Build a verification ladder from low-consequence usefulness review to high-consequence authoritative evidence and approval.
Ask learners to name the evidence that would actually prove their highest-consequence claim.
Allow two minutes to complete a claim-to-evidence row.
Walk through task, context, prompt, model, tool, and review failures before choosing a change.
Explain controlled comparison using the same representative cases and one intentional change.
Check that the learner can distinguish a single corrected example from measured workflow improvement.
Guide the learner through claim verification, cause classification, one change, and a three-case comparison.
Begin the check after the learner records both improvement and any regression or remaining uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest check for a current product-limit claim?
choices: The model's confidence
A second paraphrase
An undated forum comment
The current authoritative product documentation and, when possible, direct observation
questions.explanation: Volatile product claims need current primary evidence and direct testing when practical.

questions.prompt: How should verification change as consequences increase?
choices: It should add stronger evidence, independent review, expertise, and approval boundaries
It should become less visible
It should rely more on confidence
It should remove failure handling
questions.explanation: Higher-consequence work justifies more independent and authoritative checks.

questions.prompt: A response omits a fact that was never supplied. What should be diagnosed first?
choices: Only the model
The color of the interface
Whether the objective or context was incomplete
The length of the final answer
questions.explanation: Missing requirements or context can cause the miss even when the prompt wording is polished.

questions.prompt: What is the fairest way to compare a prompt revision?
choices: Use only a new easy example
Run old and new versions on the same representative normal and boundary cases
Change the prompt, model, tools, and rubric simultaneously
Judge whichever answer is longer
questions.explanation: Controlled comparison reveals improvements and regressions attributable to the change.

questions.prompt: When is a prompt change an improvement?
choices: When one response sounds better
When it contains more instructions
When verification is no longer needed
When representative evaluation shows the intended gain without unacceptable regression
questions.explanation: Measured performance across representative cases is stronger evidence than one anecdote.
